name: Kodama's General Relativistic Kink
description: A static wormhole held open by a ghost scalar field with a quartic potential, found numerically by Takeshi Kodama in 1978. The field sits in one vacuum far out on one side of the throat and in the other vacuum far out on the other side, so the throat carries a kink of the $\lambda\phi^4$ model. Both sides are asymptotically flat, the mass is positive, and there is neither a horizon nor a singularity.
convention: The field $S$ is dimensionless, its kinetic term has the opposite of the usual sign, and its potential is $V = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\mu/f\right)^2\left(1 - f^2S^2\right)^2$, with $\mu$ an inverse length and $f$ a pure number. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.
history: A kink is a field that sits in one vacuum far to the left and in another far to the right, with a smooth step between them [kodama1978preprint, kodama1979preprint]. The simplest lives in the $\lambda\phi^4$ model, whose field has two vacua [kodama1979preprint]. No smooth change in between brings a kink back to a vacuum [kodama1978preprint]. In three dimensions, a static, round lump of such a field with no singularity is forbidden whenever the potential is positive [kodama1978preprint].¶Takeshi Kodama, at the Centro Brasileiro de Pesquisas Físicas in Rio de Janeiro, placed the second vacuum in a second asymptotically flat space [kodama1978preprint, kodama1978]. By January 1978 his two spaces met at a throat, like the bridge of Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen through Schwarzschild's geometry [kodama1978preprint, einstein1935]. His field $S$ has the potential $V = \tfrac{1}{2}(\mu/f)^2(1 - f^2S^2)^2$, which vanishes in the two vacua $S = \pm 1/f$ [kodama1978preprint]. Far out on one side the field sits at $S = -1/f$, far out on the other at $S = +1/f$, and it passes through zero at the throat [kodama1978preprint]. With the usual sign his equations have no solution, so Kodama's field is a ghost, with negative energy in flat space [kodama1978preprint]. Homer Ellis had held a throat open with such a field five years before, a massless one with no potential [ellis1973].¶Yet the kink and the curved space around it have a positive mass [kodama1978]. Two numbers fix the whole solution, $\mu$ and $f$, and the radius of the throat comes out of the equations with no constant left to choose [kodama1978preprint]. The length $1/\mu$ sets the size of the kink, and $f$ sets its mass [kodama1978preprint]. Kodama found the solutions numerically, on the IBM 370 at the computer centre of his institute [kodama1978preprint]. Below $f \approx 0.645$ he found none, though he could not confirm it "because of the computational difficulty" [kodama1978preprint]. Clocks at the throat run slow but never stop, so the throat is no horizon, and the geometry is free of singularities [kodama1978preprint, kodama1978].¶Kodama, L. C. S. de Oliveira and Filadelfo C. Santos then measured the radius by proper distance through the throat, where every function is smooth [kodama1979preprint]. In that coordinate they shook the kink along its radius, found no mode that grows, and judged it stable against radial perturbations [kodama1979, kodama1979preprint]. A light signal can cross the bridge from one sheet to the other, and the flux of any field can follow it [kodama1979preprint]. A flux running through looks like a charged particle from one sheet and like its antiparticle from the other [kodama1979preprint]. They imagined the universe as two sheets joined by many such bridges, each one a particle or an antiparticle [kodama1979preprint]. They traced the picture to John Archibald Wheeler and thanked him for his "warm encouragement" [kodama1979preprint].¶At the University of Constantine in Algeria, Gérard Clément gave such solitons an electric charge, and with the charge set to zero they are Kodama's kink [clement1981emh, clement1981berlin]. Seen from far away, his soliton is an extended charged particle whose mass can be as small a fraction of its charge as one likes [clement1981emh]. Radial stability was not enough for him, since a kink wobbling as a dipole or a quadrupole could shed electromagnetic or gravitational waves [clement1981berlin]. Kodama, de Oliveira and Santos had held the radius of the throat fixed while they shook the kink [kodama1979preprint, dzhunushaliev2013]. When Vladimir Dzhunushaliev, Vladimir Folomeev, Burkhard Kleihaus and Jutta Kunz let the throat breathe as well, in 2013, they found a mode that grows for every size of throat, so the kink is unstable [dzhunushaliev2013].

related.text: The wormhole Homer Ellis and Kirill Bronnikov found in 1973, held open by a ghost field with no mass and no potential [ellis1973, bronnikov1973]. Kodama's ghost field has a potential with two vacua, one on each side of the throat [kodama1978preprint].
Michael Morris and Kip Thorne's static wormhole, with any redshift function and any shape function [morris1988]. In Kodama's kink both functions are fixed by the ghost field [kodama1978preprint].

Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen's bridge between two copies of Schwarzschild's exterior, the geometry Kodama set his throat beside [einstein1935, kodama1978preprint]. His throat has no horizon, and a light signal can cross it [kodama1979preprint].

Another ball of scalar field held together by its own gravity and known only as numbers [liebling2023]. There the field turns in phase about a regular centre; here a ghost field sits still across a throat [kodama1978preprint].

coordinates.name: Areal Radius

parameters.description: Redshift function, dimensionless: a clock held at radius $r$ runs at $e^{\eta}$ of the rate $t$ counts, and it approaches $0$ far away. For the kink it is known only numerically, from $\partial_r\eta = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{e^{2\alpha} - 1}{r} + r\left(e^{2\alpha}V - \left(\partial_r S\right)^2\right)\right]$

Radial function, dimensionless: $e^{\alpha}dr$ is the proper distance along the radius, and $e^{-2\alpha}$ vanishes at the throat. For the kink it is known only numerically, from $\partial_r\alpha = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1 - e^{2\alpha}}{r} - r\left(\left(\partial_r S\right)^2 + e^{2\alpha}V\right)\right]$
Areal radius of the throat, a length, the least areal radius on either side; it is fixed by $\mu$ and $f$

coordinates.convention: We use Kodama's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ on either side of the throat, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius, and leave $\eta$ and $\alpha$ free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Proper Radial Distance

parameters.description: Redshift function, dimensionless, the $\eta$ of the areal chart read along the proper distance: a clock held at $R$ runs at $e^{h}$ of the rate $t$ counts. For the kink it is known only numerically, even about the throat and approaching $0$ far away, from $2r\,\partial_R r\,\partial_R h = 1 - \left(\partial_R r\right)^2 + r^2\left(V - \left(\partial_R S\right)^2\right)$

Areal radius, a length, even about the throat, where it takes its least value $r(0) = r_0$. For the kink it is known only numerically, from $2r\,\partial_R^2r = 1 - \left(\partial_R r\right)^2 + r^2\left(\left(\partial_R S\right)^2 + V\right)$
Areal radius of the throat, a length, the least value of $r(R)$; it is fixed by $\mu$ and $f$

We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
